overview: Computer Vision enables machines to interpret and understand visual information. This module covers image representation fundamentals and image classification — the foundational CV task.
Understanding how computers 'see' images is essential before building vision models. We explore color models, image formats, preprocessing, and the complete classification pipeline.

topics.title: Image Representation
theory: Digital images are 3D tensors of shape (Height, Width, Channels). A 1920×1080 RGB image has shape (1080, 1920, 3) with 6.2 million values.
RGB color model: each pixel has Red, Green, Blue values 0-255. White=(255,255,255), Black=(0,0,0). Grayscale uses single channel with weighted average: Gray = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B.
Other color spaces: HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) — better for color-based segmentation. LAB (Lightness, A, B) — perceptually uniform. YCbCr — used in JPEG compression.
Normalization: Scale 0-255 to 0-1 for neural networks. Standardization: (x - mean) / std for zero mean, unit variance. Critical for model training.
visualIntuition: Interactive pixel explorer: hover to see RGB values. Channel separation showing R, G, B as separate grayscale images. 3D tensor visualization.
visualSuggestions: Color space converter with live preview
Resolution pyramid showing quality vs size tradeoff

topics.title: Image Preprocessing
theory: Resizing: Neural networks often require fixed input size (e.g., 224×224). Methods: nearest neighbor (fast, blocky), bilinear (smooth), bicubic (highest quality).
Data augmentation artificially expands training data: random flips, rotations, crops, brightness/contrast changes. Reduces overfitting and improves generalization.
Batch processing: Images processed in batches for efficiency. Tensor shape becomes (Batch, Height, Width, Channels) — e.g., (32, 224, 224, 3).
File formats: JPEG (lossy, smaller files), PNG (lossless, larger), TIFF (professional). Bit depth: 8-bit (256 levels) standard, 16-bit for medical/scientific.
visualIntuition: Augmentation showcase: original image surrounded by augmented versions (flipped, rotated, color-jittered).

topics.title: Image Classification Pipeline
theory: Classification assigns a label from predefined categories to an entire image. Input: image tensor. Output: probability distribution over classes.
Pipeline: Input → Preprocessing (resize, normalize) → Feature Extraction (CNN layers) → Classification (dense + softmax) → Output probabilities.
Loss function: Categorical cross-entropy measures prediction error. For true class c with predicted probability p_c: Loss = -log(p_c). Punishes confident wrong predictions.
Common architectures: Simple CNN (for learning), VGG (simple but many params), ResNet (deep with skip connections), MobileNet (efficient), EfficientNet (state-of-art).
visualIntuition: Classification pipeline animation: image flows through network layers, feature maps shown, final bar chart of class probabilities.

code.content:
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers, models

def build_classifier(input_shape=(224, 224, 3), num_classes=10):
    model = models.Sequential([
        # Feature extraction
        layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', input_shape=input_shape),
        layers.BatchNormalization(),
        layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),
        layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'),
        layers.BatchNormalization(),
        layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),
        layers.Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'),
        layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
        
        # Classification
        layers.Dense(256, activation='relu'),
        layers.Dropout(0.5),
        layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')
    ])
    
    model.compile(
        optimizer='adam',
        loss='categorical_crossentropy',
        metrics=['accuracy']
    )
    return model

topics.title: Evaluation and Metrics
theory: Accuracy: Correct predictions / Total predictions. Misleading for imbalanced classes. Use balanced accuracy or per-class metrics.
Confusion matrix: N×N table for N classes. Entry (i,j) = count of class i predicted as j. Reveals which classes are confused.
Precision (per class): Of predicted positives, how many are correct? Recall: Of actual positives, how many found? F1: Harmonic mean of precision and recall.
Top-K accuracy: True label in top K predictions? Essential for large class sets (ImageNet: 1000 classes, Top-5 used).
visualIntuition: Interactive confusion matrix heatmap. Click cell to see example misclassified images.
visualSuggestions: t-SNE/UMAP feature visualization colored by class

topics.title: Transfer Learning
theory: Training from scratch requires massive data and compute. Transfer learning leverages pretrained models (trained on ImageNet with 1.2M images).
Process: Load pretrained model → Remove final classification layer → Add new layer for your classes → Fine-tune on your data.
Feature extraction: Freeze pretrained layers, only train new classification head. Fast, works with small datasets.
Fine-tuning: Unfreeze some/all pretrained layers, train with low learning rate. Better accuracy but needs more data. Risk of catastrophic forgetting.
visualIntuition: Pretrained network with locked layers (blue) and trainable classifier (green). Data flowing through frozen feature extractor.

code.content:
from tensorflow.keras.applications import ResNet50
from tensorflow.keras import layers, models

# Load pretrained ResNet50 (without top classification layer)
base_model = ResNet50(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(224, 224, 3))

# Freeze pretrained layers
base_model.trainable = False

# Add custom classification head
model = models.Sequential([
    base_model,
    layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
    layers.Dense(256, activation='relu'),
    layers.Dropout(0.5),
    layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')
])

model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

# Train only the new layers
model.fit(train_data, epochs=10)

# Optional: Fine-tune by unfreezing some layers
base_model.trainable = True
for layer in base_model.layers[:-20]:  # Freeze all except last 20 layers
    layer.trainable = False

model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-5), loss='categorical_crossentropy')

topics.title: YOLO Object Detection
theory:
**YOLO (You Only Look Once)** is a single-stage object detector that processes the entire image in one forward pass — no region proposal stage. This makes it extremely fast, suitable for real-time applications.

**Key concepts:**
- Divides image into S×S grid cells
- Each cell predicts B bounding boxes (x, y, w, h, confidence) + class probabilities
- Uses anchor boxes: predefined aspect ratios that guide initial predictions
- Loss = localization loss + confidence loss + classification loss

**YOLOv8 (Ultralytics):** State-of-art. Keypoints, segmentation, classification, and detection in one framework.

**Real-time performance:** YOLOv8-nano runs at 100+ FPS on consumer GPUs.

**mAP (Mean Average Precision):** Standard metric for object detection. mAP@50 uses IoU threshold 0.5; mAP@50:95 averages over IoU thresholds 0.5 to 0.95.

topics.title: U-Net Semantic Segmentation
theory:
**U-Net** is an encoder-decoder architecture with **skip connections** for pixel-wise segmentation. It was designed for medical imaging but is now the standard for any dense prediction task.

**Architecture:**
1. **Encoder (contracting path):** Repeated Conv-ReLU-Pool blocks → increasing channels, decreasing resolution
2. **Bottleneck:** Deepest convolution block at lowest resolution
3. **Decoder (expanding path):** Repeated Upsample-Conv blocks → decreasing channels, increasing resolution
4. **Skip connections:** Concatenate encoder features to decoder features at matching resolutions

**Why skip connections matter:** The encoder loses fine spatial detail through pooling. Skip connections give the decoder access to high-resolution features for precise boundary localisation.

**Loss functions:**
- Cross-entropy (per-pixel classification)
- Dice Loss (overlap-based, handles class imbalance)
- Focal Loss (emphasises hard examples)

code.content:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class DoubleConv(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_ch, out_ch):
        super().__init__()
        self.block = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_ch, out_ch, 3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_ch),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(out_ch, out_ch, 3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_ch),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.block(x)

class UNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_ch=3, out_ch=1, features=[64, 128, 256, 512]):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoders = nn.ModuleList()
        self.decoders = nn.ModuleList()
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)
        
        # Encoder
        for f in features:
            self.encoders.append(DoubleConv(in_ch, f))
            in_ch = f
        
        # Bottleneck
        self.bottleneck = DoubleConv(features[-1], features[-1] * 2)
        
        # Decoder
        for f in reversed(features):
            self.decoders.append(nn.ConvTranspose2d(f*2, f, 2, stride=2))
            self.decoders.append(DoubleConv(f*2, f))
        
        self.final = nn.Conv2d(features[0], out_ch, 1)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        skip_connections = []
        for enc in self.encoders:
            x = enc(x)
            skip_connections.append(x)
            x = self.pool(x)
        x = self.bottleneck(x)
        skip_connections = skip_connections[::-1]
        for i in range(0, len(self.decoders), 2):
            x = self.decoders[i](x)  # upsample
            skip = skip_connections[i // 2]
            x = torch.cat([skip, x], dim=1)  # skip connection
            x = self.decoders[i+1](x)  # double conv
        return self.final(x)

model = UNet(in_ch=3, out_ch=1)
x = torch.randn(1, 3, 256, 256)
print(f'Input:  {x.shape}')
print(f'Output: {model(x).shape}')  # [1, 1, 256, 256]

visualSuggestions: U-shaped diagram showing encoder-decoder with skip connection arrows
Feature map resolution progression through the U-shape
visualIntuition: U-Net is shaped like the letter U. The left side zooms out — abstracting 'what is in the image'. The right side zooms back in — locating 'where exactly'. The skip connections are like stepping stones across the U, carrying fine details from the zoom-out to the zoom-in side.

topics.title: GradCAM — Visual Explanations
theory:
**GradCAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping)** visualizes which regions of an input image are most important for a specific prediction. It produces a heatmap overlay showing where the model 'looks'.

**Algorithm:**
1. Forward pass → get class prediction
2. Backward pass → compute gradients of class score w.r.t. final conv layer activations
3. Global average pool the gradients → importance weight per channel (αk)
4. Weight the activation maps by αk and sum → raw heatmap
5. Apply ReLU (only positive influence) → resize to input dimensions

**Key insight:** Each channel in the final conv layer represents a different learned pattern (edges, textures, object parts). The gradient tells you how much each pattern contributed to the specific class prediction.

**Use cases:** Debugging model mistakes, validating that models focus on correct features, building trust in clinical/safety-critical applications.

code.content:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torchvision.models as models
import torchvision.transforms as T
import numpy as np

def grad_cam(model, input_tensor, target_class, target_layer):
    """Compute GradCAM heatmap."""
    activations, gradients = {}, {}
    
    def fwd_hook(module, inp, out):
        activations['value'] = out.detach()
    def bwd_hook(module, grad_in, grad_out):
        gradients['value'] = grad_out[0].detach()
    
    fwd_h = target_layer.register_forward_hook(fwd_hook)
    bwd_h = target_layer.register_full_backward_hook(bwd_hook)
    
    output = model(input_tensor)
    model.zero_grad()
    
    one_hot = torch.zeros_like(output)
    one_hot[0, target_class] = 1
    output.backward(gradient=one_hot)
    
    fwd_h.remove(); bwd_h.remove()
    
    # Global average pool of gradients -> channel weights
    weights = gradients['value'].mean(dim=[2, 3], keepdim=True)  # (1, C, 1, 1)
    
    # Weighted sum of activations
    cam = (weights * activations['value']).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
    cam = torch.relu(cam)  # only positive influence
    cam = cam / (cam.max() + 1e-8)  # normalize
    
    return cam.squeeze().cpu().numpy()

# Usage
model = models.resnet50(weights=models.ResNet50_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V2)
model.eval()
target_layer = model.layer4[-1]  # last conv block

x = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)  # dummy input
heatmap = grad_cam(model, x, target_class=243, target_layer=target_layer)
print(f'Heatmap shape: {heatmap.shape}')  # (7, 7)
print(f'Heatmap range: [{heatmap.min():.2f}, {heatmap.max():.2f}]')

visualSuggestions: Heatmap overlay on original image showing model attention
Side-by-side GradCAM for correct vs incorrect predictions
visualIntuition: GradCAM is like asking the model 'show me what you're looking at'. It lights up the parts of the image that most influenced the prediction — red for high importance, blue for low. If the model classifies a dog but the heatmap highlights the background, something's wrong.

quiz.question: What is the ethical concern with biased training data?
options: Models amplify and perpetuate societal biases present in historical data
quiz.explanation: ML models learn patterns from data, including discriminatory ones. If historical data reflects bias (e.g., hiring data favoring certain demographics), the model will perpetuate and potentially amplify these biases.

quiz.question: What is the difference between fairness and accuracy?
options: A model can be accurate overall but unfairly discriminate against specific groups
quiz.explanation: High overall accuracy can mask poor performance on minorities. A model might be 95% accurate overall but 70% accurate for a specific demographic group, creating unfair disparate impact.

quiz.question: Why is model transparency important for accountability?
options: It enables auditing decisions, identifying errors, and building trust with affected populations
quiz.explanation: Transparent models allow stakeholders to verify that decisions are made for legitimate reasons, identify and correct errors, comply with regulations, and maintain public trust in automated systems.

quiz.question: Why is YOLO faster than two-stage detectors like R-CNN?
options: YOLO uses a smaller image resolution
YOLO processes the entire image in a single forward pass without region proposals
YOLO only detects one object class
quiz.explanation: YOLO (You Only Look Once) predicts all bounding boxes and class probabilities in a single forward pass. Two-stage detectors first propose regions, then classify each one — two separate passes make them slower.

quiz.question: What role do skip connections play in U-Net?
options: They carry high-resolution encoder features to the decoder for precise boundary localisation
They reduce the number of parameters
quiz.explanation: Skip connections concatenate encoder features with decoder features at matching resolutions. This gives the decoder access to fine spatial details that were lost during the encoder's downsampling, enabling precise pixel-level segmentation.

quiz.question: What does GradCAM use to determine which image regions are important?
options: The gradients of the class score flowing back to the final convolutional layer
quiz.explanation: GradCAM computes the gradient of a target class score with respect to the feature maps of a convolutional layer. These gradients are globally averaged to produce importance weights for each feature map channel.
